items.definition: The way a person comes back down from activation and can choose again.
items.example: His recovery took the whole walk home, and the call waited until then.

items.definition: Putting a feeling into words as a way of getting the body back down.
items.example: The venting helped her settle, and the other person had heard none of it.

items.definition: Holding a feeling down so that nothing of it shows to the other person.
items.example: Her suppression looked like calm, and the calm was read as indifference.

items.definition: Changing the story you tell about an event so that the feeling loses its grip.
items.example: His reappraisal was honest: the message had been sent late, and it was not about her.

items.definition: Turning the same thought over again and again without moving towards an action.
items.example: Her rumination ran for days, and the argument she started was never the one she had been thinking about.

items.definition: The gap between what two people in a relationship each expect, when neither has said it aloud.
items.example: The expectation mismatch was about phone calls, and it had been there for months.

items.definition: A deliberate act of bringing the body back to a calm state before you act on a strong feeling.
items.example: Grounding gave her the pause she needed before she answered him.

items.definition: An acknowledgement that another person's feeling makes sense from their point of view.
items.example: Validation is not agreement: I can see why that hurt you, without changing his mind.

items.definition: An agreed action that puts a relationship back on track after something broke between two people.
items.example: Their repair was simple: they agreed to talk again the next evening.

items.definition: The ability to make things happen, whether or not the people affected agree.
items.example: The power to shut the line down was in his hands, and it did not need anybody's permission.

items.definition: A pressure tactic that puts the decision in the hands of an expert, real or claimed.
items.example: It used authority: the technician said the part was safe, and showed no manual.

items.definition: Authority whose basis can be named and questioned, such as checked knowledge, a defined role or a rule that applies to everybody.
items.example: It was legitimate authority: she showed the standard and said who had signed the rule.

items.definition: Power that belongs to an office or an organisation rather than to a person, and passes on with the role.
items.example: Institutional power is why the badge opens the door even though the badge is not the man.

items.definition: The pressure to return a favour that the other side has given you.
items.example: The discount was the favour, and the renewal at the same price was the bill.

items.definition: The habit of giving way to authority without asking for the reason.
items.example: Deference is not weakness, but a room full of deference has nobody left to check anything.

items.definition: Any effect one person has on another, from a request to advice, in either direction.
items.example: Influence is not a privilege: the newest member of the team influences the oldest one as well.

items.definition: An honest attempt to win agreement, in which the other person is free to say no.
items.example: That was persuasion, not pressure: he explained the plan and left the decision to her.

items.definition: The removal of a real choice by force or by the threat of harm.
items.example: Sign the form today or lose the job — that is coercion, not persuasion.

items.definition: The arrangement of roles that says who decides and who answers for the decision.
items.example: The hierarchy is clear on paper; the account, the invoice and the parts were not.

items.definition: The formal authority to act, together with the limits that bound it.
items.example: His mandate was to negotiate the price, not to sign the contract.

items.definition: The condition that the reasons for a decision are visible and can be checked by the people affected.
items.example: Transparency was missing: nobody could say which number the decision was based on.

items.definition: The rules a decision must follow: notice, the chance to be heard, a written reason and a way to appeal.
items.example: Without due process the decision was final, and there was nowhere to take it.

items.definition: The answer you owe for an act, to the people affected and to the law.
items.example: The mistake was hers, and the accountability was hers as well.

items.definition: A rule about what a category of people is expected to do.
items.example: The gender role said the man pays, and the rule was never written down.

items.definition: The sense a person has of their own gender.
items.example: Her gender identity was hers to say, and nobody in the room had a vote on it.

items.definition: How a person presents their gender through clothes, voice, gesture and behaviour.
items.example: His gender expression changed when he started a new job, and the fit got easier.

items.definition: A belief about a group that is applied to a person without looking at that person.
items.example: That sentence about men and women is a stereotype, and it settles nothing about the man in front of you.

items.definition: A rule about what people should do.
items.example: It is a prescriptive norm: the expectation, not a description of what happens.

items.definition: What the people around you actually do, whether or not it is written down.
items.example: The descriptive norm here is that the whole team stays for the handover, and the expectation follows the team.

items.definition: The pattern in which one form of manliness becomes the standard everybody is measured against.
items.example: Hegemonic masculinity sets the picture of the man who never complains, and the man who does is treated as a smaller version of it.

items.definition: A situation in which a person is given two rules that cannot both be satisfied.
items.example: A double bind: be the one who decides, and be the one who notices that everybody is exhausted.

items.definition: The work of keeping other people fed, rested, healthy and connected.
items.example: Care work is the appointments, the meals and the phone calls, and it is still work.

items.definition: The work of managing your own feelings and other people's feelings so that the situation keeps running.
items.example: Emotional labour is the invisible work of keeping a meeting calm.

items.definition: The member of a couple who is expected to be the main earner.
items.example: As the breadwinner he carried the risk, and the risk became the whole family's.

items.definition: The work of running the house: cleaning, shopping, cooking, laundry and bills.
items.example: Household labour is the part of the week that never appears on a report.

items.definition: The strain that appears when one person is expected to be two things at once and the two pull in different directions.
items.example: The role conflict was not a failure of effort; two jobs had been given to one week.

items.definition: The talk in which two people change or confirm the roles they play together.
items.example: Role negotiation is not a quarrel about who is right; it is a decision about who does what.

items.definition: The phrase for the idea that time passes in the body as well as in the calendar, and that a window is closing.
items.example: The biological clock is a phrase, and the window it names is mostly a story.

items.definition: The way the reproductive system changes as a person gets older.
items.example: Reproductive ageing is gradual, and it is not the same for everybody.

items.definition: The stretch of future time a person is thinking about when they make a plan.
items.example: Their time horizon was ten years ahead; mine was two.
